title: Response rises with dose, up to a maximum

segs.text: Module seven B, objective one. How the response rises with dose, up to a maximum. Pharmacokinetics, P K, relates the drug concentration to time, and pharmacodynamics, P D, relates the concentration at the site of action, the receptor, to the pharmacologic response that is observed. She said, Pharmacodynamics is the relationship between drug concentration and pharmacological response. The link between them is also called the exposure response, concentration response or concentration effect relationship, and it is used in drug approval to judge safety, efficacy and benefit risk, and to derive dosing information.

card.m: PK: concentration against time
PD: concentration at the receptor → observed response
PK–PD = exposure-response = concentration-response = concentration-effect
drug approval: safety, efficacy, benefit-risk, dosing

segs.text: As the dose increases, the concentration at the receptor site increases, and the response increases, but only up to a maximum effect, E max. The maximum comes when all the receptors are saturated, that is, all are occupied by drug. Past that point a higher dose still raises the concentration at the receptor site, but with no free receptors left the response does not rise. Plotted against dose on an ordinary axis, the response rises steeply at low doses and then flattens. So the same added dose gives a large gain in response at low doses, where many receptors are free, and the smallest gain near the maximum.

card.m: dose higher → concentration at the receptor higher → response higher, up to E<sub>max</sub>
E<sub>max</sub>: all receptors saturated
past saturation: concentration still rises, response does not
ordinary dose axis: steep, then flat
same dose step: large gain low, smallest gain near E<sub>max</sub>

segs.text: Plotted against the log of the dose, the dose response data form a sigmoid, an S shaped curve, flat at the bottom, steep in the middle and flat at the top. The top of the S is the maximum, where the receptors are saturated. The middle of the S is close to a straight line, so there the effect, E, is a straight line function of the log of the concentration, C: E equals m log C plus e, with m the slope and e a constant. A larger m means a larger change in effect for each tenfold change in concentration.

card.m: log dose axis: sigmoid (S) curve
top: all receptors saturated
middle: E = m log C + e, slope m
m larger → more effect per tenfold change in C

segs.text: After an I V bolus the concentration falls by the same fraction each hour, so its log falls in a straight line. In the straight middle of the S curve, the effect is m log C plus a constant, so it also falls in a straight line, the same amount each hour. The relation is E equals E zero minus k m t over two point three, where E is the effect at t hours, E zero the effect at time zero, k the elimination rate constant per hour, and m the slope. k and m are both on the top, so faster elimination or a steeper slope makes the effect fall by more each hour. The two point three is there because the effect line uses base ten logs.

card.m: log C = log C<sub>0</sub> − {{frac:kt|2.3}}
E = m log C + e → a straight line in time
E = E<sub>0</sub> − {{frac:kmt|2.3}}
k in hr<sup>−1</sup>, t in hr, m = slope of E against log C
k or m larger → effect falls faster
2.3: base-10 logs

segs.text: On a plasma level against time curve, the effect is read against the minimum effective concentration, M E C or C eff, the lowest level at which it appears. Onset is the time at which the rising level first reaches the M E C. She said, when does the drug reach a therapeutic concentration? That's our onset. Duration is how long the level stays at or above the M E C, a time, and intensity is how far the peak rises above it, a difference of two concentrations. Above the minimum toxic concentration, M T C, toxicity appears, and the range from the M E C to the M T C is the therapeutic window.

card.m: read against the MEC (C<sub>eff</sub>), a concentration
onset: the level first reaches the MEC
duration (t<sub>eff</sub>): time at or above the MEC, in hr
intensity: peak concentration minus MEC, in mg/L
therapeutic window: MEC to MTC

segs.text: In the concept items, the response is not proportional to the dose; it rises to a maximum, and the same added dose gives the smallest gain near that maximum. The response stops rising because all receptors are saturated, not because the concentration stops rising or elimination speeds up. Against log dose the curve is an S; rising steeply and then flattening is the shape against dose on an ordinary axis. In the effect line, m is a slope, not a mass or a concentration, and the effect falls in a straight line, not by a fixed fraction each hour. Absolute bioavailability is a P K comparison, not a use of exposure response information. Onset, intensity and duration depend on the dose and the pharmacokinetics; objective two works out duration.

card.m: not proportional at every dose: up to a maximum
smallest gain: near the maximum
reason: receptors saturated
log axis: S. ordinary axis: steep, then flat
m: a slope. effect: straight line in time
absolute bioavailability: a PK comparison
onset, intensity, duration: depend on dose and PK → objective two
